newsitem.title: GERMANY: German investors edge towards equity culture.
newsitem.headline: German investors edge towards equity culture.

text.p: The battle to lure coy investors into equities continues in Germany, with a New Market for small growth stocks providing the latest string to the bourse's increasingly sophisticated bow.

German investors lag behind their Anglo-Saxon counterparts when it comes to investing in equities, holding only around six percent of their total assets in shares. Instead they tend to follow the fixed-income route and buy bonds.
However, there are signs that both private and institutional investors are starting to take equities more seriously.

Initiatives such as the New Market for growth stocks, big-name initial public offers including the 20-billion-mark Deutsche Telekom flotation, and the increased visibility of equity funds have breathed new life into Germany's cautious investment world.

Recent figures from Dresdner Bank's investment group DBI showed that 70 percent of investments in funds in the early part of 1997 went into equity funds, which also provided the highest returns in the period.
In an attempt to increase levels of liquidity, the German bourse in March set up the New Market, modelled on New York's NASDAQ exchange, with 20 companies expected to list in its first year.
So far two have listed -- mobile phone services firm MobilCom and engineering services group Bertrandt.
Would-be members of the New Market have to meet strict entry requirements on issue conditions and transparency. They must publish quarterly results and use International Accounting Standards.

"Conceptually it's a great idea. Anything providing easier access to the German capital markets is a good thing. At the same time, it's too early to tell how successful it will be," said Robert Willis, analyst at Schroder Securities in London.
"We need to see if any real companies of substance come to the market and we need to see these companies attracting sustained liquidity," said Willis.
Jochen Waiblinger, assistant vice president of equities at BHF Bank in Frankfurt, agrees.

"It's a start, and a good one at that. Obviously we have to wait to see how the market develops, but if we get decent liquidity in the stocks then it will be attractive to fund managers. But don't expect any immediate impact in the first six or nine months," said Waiblinger.
Analysts say Germany's government is under tremendous pressure to provide retirement funds for its greying population.

The debate on pension provision is centred on whether the current system, which is dominated by pay-as-you-go government schemes, will have to be supplemented with a funded pension system and how this can be brought about.
So far Bonn has failed to implement reforms aimed at encouraging the growth of private pension plans.

Jan Nyholm, head of Fidelity Investments in Germany, which has been aggressively wooing the German investor of late, said that impetus has to come from the legislative side if there is to be a real upswing in the amounts flowing into equity funds.
"But we are not expecting a big bang," Nyholm said at a Munich conference on share culture and fund management in Germany.

Waiblinger said: "Private pension funds will definitely become more important. We are coming from nowhere, but there is tremendous catch-up potential there, which is favourable for the German stock market in general."
"Equities have a good future here, and fund management especially, but don't look too short-term," said Waiblinger.
